sections.h2: Where to get help and how to pay
sections.html:
Guilford County's Tax Department sets values and mails bills. Walk-in help is available at 400 W. Market St. in Greensboro and 325 E. Russell Ave. in High Point, weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

  • Pay It portal, online or at (336) 203-7795: a 1.85% electronic fee plus a $2 transaction fee.
  • Mailed checks: payable to Guilford County Tax Department, sent to the Charlotte lockbox at P.O. Box 70939, zip 28272-0939.
  • Counter payments: cash, checks and cards, with card payers adding 2.35% plus $2. Gift cards cannot be used.

Mailed payments are timed by postmark. With no Postal Service postmark, the day the office receives the envelope counts, and you must prove it was on time.

Bills for 2026 carried 2025 values, so the reappraisal numbers debut on the 2027 bill. Senate Bill 889 put a one-year hold on the reappraisal that began January 1, 2026, and Guilford is covered.

Staff appraisers did the reappraisal work themselves, and owners received notices in February 2026. The next reappraisal year is 2032.

If you already appealed the 2026 value, that appeal stays alive and carries to the next bill. Commissioners set the fiscal year 2026-27 rate at 78.95 cents per $100, which is 5.9 cents higher than before. The rate rose in 2026 while the new values arrive in 2027, so the two changes land in different years.

September 1 is the day a bill is payable, and a payment on or before January 5 owes no interest. Bills go out in the first half of July.

A prepayment discount rewards owners who pay by August 31. The percentage has been quoted two ways, so ask the Tax Department which figure applies to your bill.

After the cutoff, interest starts at 2% for month one and 0.75% per month beyond that. Collection steps begin immediately: garnishment of wages and bank accounts, levies on personal property, attachment of state refunds and lottery prizes, and eventually foreclosure. Guilford never runs tax lien sales.

Put the appeal in writing and send it to the Board of Equalization and Review any time from January 1 to May 15. The 5 p.m. cutoff moves to the next working day when May 15 lands on a weekend or holiday. Online filing is accepted, and the paper form is available from 336-641-4814.

Under the moratorium law, 2026 appeals stay open through December 31, 2026, and 2027 appeals run to May 17, 2027. The online portal reopens January 1, 2027, and taxreval@guilfordcountync.gov can mail you a form earlier.

A county appraiser reviews the file and makes a recommendation. Accept it and the matter closes. Reject it and you get a hearing date before the five-member board, where the county value starts out presumed correct and you must bring proof. Useful proof includes:

  • Closed sales of similar homes near the reappraisal date, an appraisal from the year before, or a contractor quote that attaches a dollar figure to a defect.
  • Wrong square footage on the property record card, and outside influences like a flood zone.

The board will not act on the size of an increase or on hardship paying, and it excludes forced sales from its comparables. Further review sits with the state Property Tax Commission, which takes a notice filed within 30 days after the board mails its ruling.

Guilford administers three programs, and an owner can collect from only one. June 1 is the filing deadline. A late packet goes to the review board if the Tax Department has it a full week ahead of the board's final December session.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: shelters $25,000 or 50% of the home's value from tax, whichever is greater. You must be 65, or totally and permanently disabled, on January 1, with gross income under $38,800. It needs one application.
  • Circuit breaker: caps the yearly bill at 4% of income, or 5% when income falls between $38,800 and $58,200. Five years of owning and living in the home are required, and you reapply annually.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: shelters the first $45,000 of value with no age or income test. It serves a veteran whose service-connected disability is total and permanent, and that veteran's unmarried surviving spouse.

If you plan to sell, look hardest at the circuit breaker. Tax above the cap is postponed and stays on the parcel as a lien. Once the home changes hands, three years of postponed tax come due with interest. The exclusions carry no repayment. Mail applications to PO Box 3138 in Greensboro (27402) or hand them in at either tax office. Relief help lines are 336-641-3320 and 336-641-7911.

Pay it off no later than closing. The lien attaches to the parcel as of its January 1 listing date, with interest and penalties riding along, so a buyer's title search will turn it up.

If a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer requests the bill from the county, and a notice reaches you around mid to late July. The legal duty stays with you, so confirm the amount was paid. Without escrow, pay directly before interest starts.

Unpaid taxes can lead to a court foreclosure modeled on a mortgage foreclosure. It ends in a sale at the courthouse door, followed by ten days in which a higher bid may be filed once the commissioner reports. Selling first keeps the price with you. The Tax Department's bill search shows what is owed, and our register of deeds guide explains how the deed records afterward.

Check these before listing a Guilford house:

  • A circuit breaker deferral that comes due on transfer.
  • A parcel record that no longer matches the house after an addition. An online Property Verification form fixes this, and the record card updates in about 48 hours.
  • Vehicle gap bills, which arrive separately from the real estate bill.

A cash buyer expects clear title just as a lender does, so the tax balance gets settled the same way.

Guilford has 246,403 housing units and 562,234 residents. About 59.9% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the middle owned home is worth $259,900. Owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,536 a month, those without pay $515, and renters pay a median $1,163. Seniors make up 18.0% of the population, the group the relief programs target.

faqs.q: Were Guilford's 2026 tax bills based on the new reappraisal?
faqs.a: No, they used 2025 values because Senate Bill 889 paused the reappraisal for a year. The new values apply to the 2027 bill, appeals filed against them are still processed, and 2032 is the next reappraisal.

faqs.q: When must a Guilford property owner file a value appeal?
faqs.a: In an ordinary year the cutoff is 5 p.m. on May 15, and the appeal has to be in hand or postmarked by then. The moratorium law extended 2026 appeals to December 31, 2026 and set May 17, 2027 for 2027 appeals.

faqs.q: Is there a property tax break for seniors or a disabled veteran in Guilford County?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and under the income cap can shelter $25,000 or half the home's value, whichever is larger. A qualifying disabled veteran can shelter $45,000. File with the Tax Department by June 1.

faqs.q: What becomes due if a circuit breaker owner sells?
faqs.a: Three years of deferred tax, plus interest, come due on the transfer date, because a sale ends eligibility. Ask the Tax Department for a payoff figure before closing.

faqs.q: How can I pay the Guilford County tax bill?
faqs.a: Use the Pay It portal online or by phone, mail a check, or visit the Greensboro or High Point office. Cards add a fee, and gift cards are refused.
